contributions.headingText: Paediatric nodal marginal zone lymphoma (PNMZL) is a primary nodal mature B-cell neoplasm, mostly occurring in the head and neck region of adolescent boys. PNMZL shares the interfollicular expansion of clonal marginal zone B cells with usual nodal marginal zone lymphoma (NMZL). Nevertheless, it has specific clinical and histomorphological features that differ from those of the adult counterpart.
9699/3 Paediatric nodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma
2A85.Y Further specified mature B-cell neoplasms or lymphoma
Not recommended: monocytoid B-cell lymphoma; parafollicular B-cell lymphoma.
PNMZL often involves lymph nodes of the head and neck region (i.e. cervical, submandibular, and supraclavicular lymph nodes) {28771659; 29286565; 32452165; 31104676; 31187530}.

Patients with PNMZL usually present with peripheral lymphadenopathy without clinical symptoms, localized stage I/II disease {32452165}, and normal serum LDH levels {28771659; 29286565; 32452165; 12657939; 31187530}. However, stage III/IV disease at presentation has been reported, emphasizing the need for complete staging {28771659; 29286565; 32452165; 31187530; 26728447}. Splenic and extranodal marginal zone lymphomas (MZLs) are very rare in the paediatric age group and should not be considered in this category.

Imaging

Sonography and MRI usually confirm the localized disease and could inform the surgeon on the possibility of a complete resection {25940716}.

The overall incidence of PNMZL among childhood non-Hodgkin lymphoma is < 2%. It is most commonly diagnosed in otherwise healthy adolescent boys (median age: 16 years) {12657939; 28771659; 29286565; 32452165; 20305621; 27338637} and rarely in adults {19863176; 15754298}.

In contrast to extranodal MZL, PNMZL occurs extremely rarely in patients with pre-existing immunodeficiencies or autoimmune disorders, or in association with an infectious stimulus {8980374; 28771659; 29286565; 32452165; 16123999; 3141260; 3136072; 26740867; 16397126; 12657939; 30371536; 16321869; 29408337}.

The pathogenetic mechanisms underlying the development of PNMZL are currently unknown, mainly owing to the hitherto very limited molecular studies. In adult NMZL, studies on the IGHV gene mutation status suggest that the lymphoma may originate from different subsets of marginal zone B cells: the naïve B cells expressing unmutated IGHV genes and the somatically hypermutated antigen-experienced B cells {10088550; 28288716; 11468179; 31802229; 15820942}. No evidence of EBV or bacterial infections have been documented in PNMZL {8980374; 12657939; 25625642; 25722108}.

Like in NMZL, trisomy 18 has been found in 21% of PNMZL cases, with 1 case showing concomitant trisomy 3 {20305621}. Trisomy 13, monosomy 20, and translocation of the IGH gene with an unknown partner gene have also been reported in single cases {8980374; 20305621; 25625642}. PNMZL lacks the t(14;18) IGH::MALT1 rearrangement as well as BCL10 and FOXP1 translocations {20305621}. A whole-exome sequencing study performed on four PNMZL cases reported isolated point mutations in genes of unknown pathogenic potential involved in cellular adhesion, cytokine regulatory elements, and cellular proliferation {27338637}. Point mutations in MAP2K1, TNFRSF14, KMT2C, IRF8, and NOTCH2 have been found in PNMZL and paediatric-type follicular lymphoma in two studies, suggesting an overlap between these two entities {35609565; 35834399}.
PNMZL appears as enlarged and encapsulated lymph nodes without sclerosis or necrosis.

The lymph node architecture is at least partly effaced by an interfollicular proliferation with markedly expanded pale marginal zones and attenuated sinuses.

Immunophenotype

Characteristically, the follicles are often enlarged, with a disrupted CD23-positive follicular dendritic cell meshwork and IgD-positive mantle cells extending into the germinal centres resembling progressively transformed germinal centres (PTGCs). However, unlike in PTGCs, the peripheral rim of IgD-positive mantle is irregular because of the infiltration of marginal zone cells. Widely spaced hyperplastic follicles partially colonized by IgD-negative cells but still containing residual typical germinal-centre cells (centrocytes and centroblasts) can also be present. Complete effacement of the lymph node architecture by a diffuse infiltration, as seen in adult NMZL, is rarely observed. The neoplastic population is represented by a polymorphic B-cell infiltrate composed of small to medium-sized B cells with monocytoid features (round nuclei, pale-staining cytoplasm) and centrocyte-like features (irregular nuclei, scant cytoplasm). Plasmacytoid cells, as well as scattered immunoblasts and centroblast-like cells, may be present {12657939; 15690646; 20305621; 26416032; 28277421; 25625642}. Sheets of large cells should not be present and would favour the diagnosis of a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The infiltrating cells may express BCL2 and in most cases are CD43-positive. BCL6 and CD10 are typically negative, although rare CD10-positive exceptions have been reported {26416032}. Proliferation is low to moderate. A cytoplasmic light chain restriction can be observed {20305621; 26416032; 28277421}.

Flow cytometry may reveal surface light chain–restricted CD19+, CD20+, CD10− B cells in both PNMZL and atypical marginal zone hyperplasia. Molecular testing for heavy and light chain rearrangements are therefore mandatory for the differential diagnosis {25625642; 19863176; 12657939; 26416032; 25722108; 20305621}.

Differential diagnosis

Cases with features overlapping between paediatric-type follicular lymphoma and PNMZL have been reported, especially in PNMZL with extensive follicular colonization and paediatric-type follicular lymphoma with marginal zone differentiation {26416032}. Differential diagnostic features in PNMZL are the expanded interfollicular areas of CD43+ marginal zone B cells, the presence of PTGC-like features, and the higher content of PD1+ T cells in the remaining germinal centres {23108024; 26416032}.

Various forms of marginal zone hyperplasia should be excluded. Polyclonal expansions of IgD+ marginal zones with cytoplasmic light chain restriction and aberrant expression of CD43 can be observed in atypical marginal zone hyperplasia, a reactive condition mainly reported in the tonsils or in the gastrointestinal tract {15256428; 25955878}. In lymph nodes, a similar condition with variable marginal zone hyperplasia, PTGC-like nodules, skewed light chain expression, and faint IgD positivity has been reported in association with Haemophilus influenzae infection {25722108}. Children with activated PI3K delta syndrome frequently present with lymphadenopathy with marked polyclonal marginal zone hyperplasia; the germinal centres, however, are commonly infiltrated by PD1+ T cells, and sometimes a few cells infected by EBV and CMV are detected {27555459; 32181277}.

A cytology-based approach for the diagnosis of PNMZL is not recommended because MZLs are composed of a polymorphic lymphoid population of centrocyte-like, monocytoid, and plasmacytoid cells that can be extremely difficult to distinguish from reactive cells on FNAB specimens {14579297; 22693682}.

Clonal rearrangements of IGH and IGK are detected in almost all cases of PNMZL. In contrast, atypical marginal zone hyperplasia can show monotypic light chain immunoglobulin expression by both immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry but an absence of clonality by molecular analyses {12657939; 25722108; 20305621; 25625642; 26416032; 8980374}. Combining morphological and immunophenotypic findings with molecular clonality assessments is therefore strongly recommended to support the diagnosis of PNMZL.

Essential: partial effacement of lymph node architecture by interfollicular proliferation and marginal zone expansion of predominant monocytoid and centrocyte-like B cells; clonal IGH and IGK gene rearrangements; immunophenotype compatible with marginal zone B cells (BCL6−, CD43+/−).

Desirable: residual follicles with PTGC-like features; follicular colonization; monotypic light chain restriction; increased PD1+ cells in reactive germinal centres.

Although most patients with PNMZL present with localized disease of the head and neck region and lack B symptoms, complete staging should be performed according to the revised International Pediatric Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma Staging System (IPNHLSS) {32452165; 25940716}. Whether analysis of the bone marrow and cerebrospinal fluid is necessary is a matter of current debate, but it might be waived in cases that are histologically and clinically typical of PNMZL {32452165}.

According to the available literature, most patients with limited-stage PNMZL underwent watchful waiting after complete resection {28771659; 29286565; 32452165; 12657939; 31187530}. Fewer than 5% of them relapsed, but these patients were cured with second-line therapy. Survival rates thus approach 100% {28771659; 29286565; 32452165; 12657939; 31187530}. Primary systemic therapy might be reserved for the very rare patients with advanced or relapsed/progressive disease. Observations of a few patients suggest that a period of delay before considering systemic therapy might be appropriate for incompletely resected localized PNMZL {28771659; 32452165}. Only a few patients with PNMZL have been primarily treated by local radiotherapy or systemic polychemotherapy; none of them relapsed {31187530}. However, in view of the high cure rates, local irradiation is not indicated.
